headline: High: gpt-engineer can write and execute code in a shared project directory while the other agent has broad network egress, creating dangerous default pathways for leakage, prompt injection, and cascading errors.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: awesome-cli-apps is a content-writing/listing agent with no shared channel documented, but gpt-engineer reads and writes the project directory and can ingest file content as part of its workflow. If A’s content is copied into B’s workspace, B may treat it as trusted instructions. The interaction is inferred, not directly documented, so uncertainty pushes upward.
conditions: IF agent_a outputs text that is copied into agent_b's project directory
IF agent_b parses file contents as instructions without provenance checks
mitigations: Keep A and B in separate directories
Require a human review step before B reads A-produced files
Prefix A outputs as data, not instructions
Disable automatic ingestion of copied text into B
requires-engineering: add provenance tagging between agents

B_data_leakage.rationale: A has broad network egress and B can read/write the project directory while handling generated source code and OPENAI_API_KEY. If sensitive files are placed in B’s workspace, either agent can move content off-box through network calls or model APIs. The shared workspace path is the main exposure; no direct evidence shows PHI, so medium fits.
conditions: IF sensitive files are stored in agent_b's project directory
IF either agent is allowed to transmit workspace contents to a remote model or API
mitigations: Do not place secrets in the shared project directory
Use a throwaway workspace for B
Rotate any exposed API keys immediately
Restrict outbound network access during runs
requires-engineering: add DLP/redaction before egress

C_capability_conflict.rationale: B has write_filesystem and per-project shared state with multiple instances; A is a content-writing agent that may also produce files or text artifacts, but its write surface is not documented. Because overlapping mutable workspace access is plausible yet not fully proven, the safer choice is medium rather than low. No locking is documented.
conditions: IF both agents operate on the same project directory
IF A’s outputs are materialized as files that B also edits
mitigations: Assign separate project directories
Serialize access with a human gate
Avoid concurrent runs on the same repo
Snapshot the workspace before each agent runs
requires-engineering: add file locking or transactional writes

D_cascading_error.rationale: gpt-engineer explicitly writes files then offers to run code, so it can act on A’s outputs if they are fed into its prompt or workspace. A is a content-writing agent, so its text can become authoritative input for B. With B’s execute_shell and spawn_subprocesses, a mistaken or malicious instruction can cascade into code execution or irreversible repo changes.
conditions: IF A’s generated text is used as B’s implementation spec
IF B is permitted to run generated code or shell commands
mitigations: Require B to cite source lines before acting
Disable auto-run of generated code
Insert a verification step between A and B
Limit B to read-only mode until review completes
requires-engineering: add policy checks before shell execution

E_compliance.rationale: B explicitly handles OPENAI_API_KEY and writes generated source code, while A’s profile shows broad network egress but no specific regulated data class. The pair does not show a residency or certification mismatch, so only a small compliance gap is evidenced: secrets could be exposed if placed in B’s workspace and then egressed by either agent.
conditions: IF secrets are stored in files that B reads
IF either agent sends those files to a third-party API
mitigations: Keep secrets out of the workspace
Use environment variables with least privilege
Redact secrets before any model call
Review retention settings for API providers
requires-engineering: document data-handling boundaries
